mas12-complex-review.title: Cartesian complex numbers and geometric interpretation
mas12-complex-review.unit: Unit 3 – Complex numbers, functions and vectors
mas12-complex-review.coverage: Lesson concept checks followed by related subject revision.

questions.prompt: Cartesian complex numbers and geometric interpretation — Which expression gives the real-plane dot product of complex vectors u,v?
questions.explanation: Expanding u times the conjugate of v yields the Cartesian dot product in its real part.

questions.prompt: Modulus, principal argument and polar conversion — What is the principal argument of a negative real number under the course convention?
questions.explanation: The interval includes positive pi and excludes negative pi; zero alone has undefined argument.

questions.prompt: Complex loci, intersections and argument restrictions — Why is the endpoint excluded from a fixed-argument ray?
options: The modulus cannot equal zero in any complex equation.
A ray must contain negative radius values.
The zero displacement has no defined argument.
All locus endpoints are always excluded.
questions.explanation: The argument is a direction of a nonzero vector.

questions.prompt: Polar products, quotients and transformations — What geometric action is multiplication by $2\operatorname{cis}(\pi/6)$?
options: Reflection in the real axis only.
Dilation factor pi/6 and rotation 2 radians.
Dilation factor 2 and anticlockwise rotation pi/6 about the origin.
questions.explanation: The modulus supplies length scale and the argument supplies directed rotation.

questions.prompt: De Moivre theorem, powers and proof — What happens to a modulus r when raising a complex number to the positive integer power n?
options: It stays r for all n.
questions.explanation: Repeated multiplication multiplies the moduli, while arguments add.

questions.prompt: All roots of a complex number — Why add $2\pi k$ before dividing the argument by n?
options: To guarantee that all roots have principal argument zero.
To generate all n distinct roots rather than one selected root.
questions.explanation: Full turns of the original argument become distinct angular positions after division.

questions.prompt: Roots of unity and regular polygons — How far apart are adjacent arguments of nth roots of unity?
questions.explanation: The n equally spaced roots divide one full turn into n parts.

questions.prompt: Factor/remainder theorems and conjugate-root polynomials — What is the remainder on division of P(z) by z-a?
questions.explanation: The division identity evaluated at z=a removes the factor term and leaves the remainder.

questions.prompt: Vector and Cartesian planes and intersections — What if a line direction is perpendicular to a plane normal?
options: The line is parallel to the plane or lies wholly in it.
It must meet the plane in exactly one point.
It is perpendicular to the plane.
questions.explanation: The anchor location decides between containment and no intersection.

questions.prompt: Cross products, area and normal vectors — What does the magnitude of u cross v measure?
options: The area of their spanned parallelogram.
questions.explanation: Its magnitude is base times perpendicular height.

questions.prompt: Parametric curves and Cartesian conics — What can be lost when eliminating a parameter?
options: The interval restriction and direction of travel.
questions.explanation: The Cartesian equation alone may describe a larger locus without traversal information.

questions.prompt: Three-dimensional components, magnitude and dot product — Which vector has no unit direction?
options: Any vector with one zero component.
Any vector with a negative component.
questions.explanation: Normalising requires division by a nonzero magnitude.

questions.prompt: Projectile and circular motion in a plane — Why can constant-speed circular motion have nonzero acceleration?
options: Constant speed always means zero velocity.
Acceleration measures only changes in speed.
questions.explanation: Acceleration is the rate of change of the full velocity vector.

questions.prompt: Geometric proofs with vector notation — What makes a proof general rather than one numerical check?
options: It uses arbitrary objects satisfying the stated hypotheses.
It uses a graph drawn to scale.
questions.explanation: General vector expressions cover every eligible configuration.

questions.prompt: Vector calculus, displacement and distance travelled — Which integral gives distance travelled?
options: The magnitude of final position in every case.
The integral of the magnitude of velocity.
The integral of one chosen velocity component.
questions.explanation: Speed is nonnegative and accumulates the full travelled path.

questions.prompt: Vector equations of lines and line segments — What extra test distinguishes coincident lines from distinct parallel lines?
options: Whether both use the same parameter letter.
Whether both direction vectors have unit length.
Whether their x coordinates are always positive.
Whether an anchor point of one lies on the other.
questions.explanation: Parallel directions allow either coincident or displaced lines.

questions.prompt: Coordinates, distance and sphere equations — What locus is equidistant from two distinct points in three dimensions?
options: Always a sphere centred at the origin.
questions.explanation: Expanding equality of squared distances produces a plane normal to their displacement.

questions.prompt: Reconstructing functions and interpreting parameters — What additional information commonly determines a scale constant after factors are fixed?
options: The colour of the plotted curve.
A valid point on the graph.
questions.explanation: A permitted point supplies an equation involving the remaining scale parameter.

questions.prompt: Rational graphs, holes and asymptotes — What remains after cancelling an original denominator factor?
options: Every cancellation creates a vertical asymptote.
Its zero remains excluded from the domain.
The excluded input is automatically restored.
questions.explanation: Simplification preserves values at admissible inputs but does not redefine the original function.

questions.prompt: Absolute-value transformations and piecewise reasoning — Which part of y=f(x) is reflected to obtain y=|f(x)|?
options: Only the right half is reflected left.
The entire graph is reflected in y=x.
The part below the x-axis is reflected upward.
questions.explanation: Absolute value of the output changes negative y-values to their positives.

questions.prompt: Partial fractions and rational integration — What should precede partial fractions for an improper rational expression?
options: Cancelling every denominator zero without checking.
Replacing all factors by a single constant.
questions.explanation: Division separates a polynomial and a proper rational remainder.

questions.prompt: Substitution and reverse chain-rule integration — After substitution, what should the transformed integral contain?
options: Only numerical constants in every case.
Only the new variable and its differential.
An arbitrary mixture of unexplained x and u terms.
questions.explanation: Every original factor must be accounted for by the substitution.

questions.prompt: Numerical integration, technology and model checks — What should accompany a numerical integral answer?
options: An assertion that every displayed digit is exact.
The mathematical integral setup, rounding and contextual units.
questions.explanation: The setup communicates what was computed and allows independent checking.

questions.prompt: Trigonometric identities before integration — Which identity is useful for integrating an even sine square?
questions.explanation: The double-angle identity converts the power to directly integrable terms.

questions.prompt: Areas between curves with either variable — For integration with respect to y, which difference gives strip width?
options: Upper boundary minus lower boundary regardless of variable.
Left minus right for positive width.
questions.explanation: Horizontal strips have width measured along the x direction.

questions.prompt: Logarithmic integrals and absolute values — What is the antiderivative of f derivative divided by nonzero f?
questions.explanation: The absolute value supplies a real logarithm on either sign interval.

questions.prompt: Solids of revolution about either axis — What is a washer cross-sectional area?
questions.explanation: It subtracts the inner disk area from the outer disk area.

questions.prompt: Substitution in definite integrals and changed bounds — When integrating entirely in u, which bounds must be used?
options: The original x-values regardless of substitution.
No bounds for a definite integral.
The transformed u-values of the original endpoints.
questions.explanation: Bounds must refer to the variable used in the antiderivative.

questions.prompt: Margin of error, sample size and sampling limits — How should a noninteger minimum sample size be rounded?
options: To the nearest integer regardless of the inequality.
questions.explanation: The completed sample size must meet or exceed the calculated lower bound.

questions.prompt: Related rates, chain rules and signed changes — When should instantaneous values normally be substituted in a related-rates equation?
options: After differentiating the general changing relation.
Before differentiation, treating every current quantity as constant.
questions.explanation: The derivatives must retain the time dependence of each changing quantity.

questions.prompt: Implicit differentiation and tangent gradients — What is the x-derivative of $y^2$ when y depends on x?
questions.explanation: The chain rule includes the derivative of the dependent variable.

questions.prompt: Separation, initial conditions and lost equilibria — What must be checked after dividing a differential equation by g(y)?
options: Whether the equation becomes second order.
questions.explanation: Dividing by a factor excludes its zeros and can remove valid equilibria.

questions.prompt: Variable acceleration and velocity–position methods — What information is missing from a formula for v squared alone?
options: The direction or sign of velocity.
questions.explanation: Both positive and negative velocities share the same square.

questions.prompt: Small increments and Euler approximation — Which slope does standard explicit Euler use for a step?
options: The slope at the current starting point.
Always the original slope for every step.
questions.explanation: The current coordinates determine the local tangent used to advance.

questions.prompt: A sample mean is a random variable — What does unbiasedness of the sample mean assert?
options: Every sample contains the entire population.
Its expectation over the sampling model equals mu.
Every sample mean equals mu exactly.
questions.explanation: Unbiasedness is a repeated-sampling property, not an exactness claim for one sample.

questions.prompt: Simple harmonic motion, phase and energy relation — Where is SHM speed largest?
options: Only when acceleration magnitude is largest.
questions.explanation: The relation v squared=omega squared times amplitude squared minus displacement squared peaks at zero displacement.

questions.prompt: Repeated-sampling confidence interpretation — In repeated confidence-interval sampling, what varies?
options: The sample statistics and interval endpoints.
The fixed population mean changes after every sample.
questions.explanation: Random samples generate different intervals around one fixed parameter.

questions.prompt: Approximate confidence intervals for a population mean — What is the margin of error in the large-sample mean interval?
options: 95% of s for every confidence level.

options: s divided by square root n.

options: The distribution of the individual population values directly.
The distribution of all possible population means.
Only one sample sorted into order.
A sampling distribution of the mean.
